figures.caption: Figure 3: SpineFM enhances generalizability via multi-modal continual training. a, SpineFM integrates slice-level pretraining (DINOv3) and sequence-level continual training. The former captures multi-scale visual features, while the latter aligns multi-modality features using clinical reports. b, Saliency maps under different training strategies. Bi-modal emphasizes less informative structural features, whereas tri-modal highlights pathology-relevant regions, with divergence increasing over training. c, AUROC differences between T1- and T2-weighted models across conditions (T1 minus T2). d–e, Cross-manufacturer and cross-cohort evaluation of SpineAgent Diagnosis Agents, respectively.

Figure 6: Medical-report-drafting performance with SpineAgent. a, Screenshot of a demo case of our online tool using SpineAgent to help with radiology-report generation. b, Representative examples of generated report drafts. c, Distribution of the RADPEER score of the in-scope cases. d, Distribution of the editing distances of the in-scope cases’ reports. e, Comparison of SpineAgent and a baseline LLaVA model, using human-corrected reports as the gold standard.

Figure 5: Retrieval performance of SpineFM compared with baseline models. a, Intra-dataset case retrieval on the internal UW Medicine cohort. b, Intra-dataset case retrieval on the external RSNA cohort. c, Cross-orientation image retrieval across different imaging planes. d, Recall @ 5 performance stratified by MRI series type, comparing models that employ the synthesizer-based visual encoder with those that do not. e, Pipeline for generating radiology report drafts from MRI series. f, Quantitative comparison of report drafting performance between SpineAgent and baseline methods.

Figure 4: Segmentation agents that localize pathological regions. a, Segmentation agents’ conditional-specific slice selection phase (left) and segmentation phase (right) find pathological regions with a 3D MRI image. Task heads differ by target condition (one of 17). b, Performance on pathological slice selection in terms of AUROC. c, Performance on segmentation in terms of the distance between curated bounding box and predicted bounding box. d, Case studies showing the pathological slice selection by different methods. e, Case studies showing the segmentation performance by different methods. Red (/green) box indicates ground truth (/predicted) box.

Figure 1: Overview of the SpineAgent framework consisting of a multi-sequence MRI foundation model SpineFM and a multi-agent framework SpineAgent for report generation. a, Our pre-training data collected at UW Medical Center contain 32,047 patients and 453,683 series, covering diverse body parts, manufacturers and patient age groups. b, SpineFM is first trained as a multi-sequence foundation model capable of encoding heterogeneous MRI inputs. It then supports a set of specialized agents that generate complementary diagnostic signals, whose outputs are integrated to guide the Medical Report Agent for final report generation.

Figure 2: Evaluation of SpineAgent on spinal condition classification across 17 conditions. a, Overview of the multi-modal continual pretraining framework of SpineFM . T1- and T2-weighted images are encoded using dedicated encoders, while other sequences are embedded via a synthesis module derived from T1 and T2 representations. b, The prevalence of the 17 conditions across four spinal regions, aligned with panels c–f. c–f, AUROC comparison of SpineAgent Diagnosis Agents and baseline models trained on T1-only, T2-only, non-T1/T2, or all sequences.
